## Findings by module

### directing-5

- **confirmed** (ch-005 neutral shot): Spoto on Champagne: the same shot of a smiling detective reads as sinister, protective, kindly then lecherous; Hitchcock insists a shot is neutral and editing and context supply meaning. Supports the Kuleshov lesson. Also Farmer's Wife: ring suspended from a saddle intercut with a wistful look conveys thought by juxtaposition, few intertitles
- **confirmed** (ch-044 storyboard): Spoto: Hitchcock plotted each film's action by storyboard sketches developed from the final shooting script and used it as a guide for himself and the cinematographer while often modifying it; abbreviations explained (L.S., P.O.V., Obj., O.S., C.U., Insert, Process). Confirms the course's storyboard and shot-list teaching, with the point that the plan may change on set
- **contradicted** (ch-025 long take limits): Spoto and Hume Cronyn: sustained long takes (Rope, Under Capricorn) were meant to be swifter but proved hard to photograph and exasperating for actors (furniture slipped away by grips as the camera approached, Bergman miserable), and without cutting the scenes lost tension and visual-narrative rhythm; a technique that fits a small story (Rope) may fail a large one. A caution against choosing a technique for its own sake
- **extended** (ch-005 silent films): Spoto: Hitchcock worked from title-card design and set design; The Lodger (1926) planned every shot and cut, kept intertitles sparse, showed sound visually (glass ceiling so the family sees pacing feet), and used elliptical montage to compress motifs; Easy Virtue tells a proposal through a switchboard operator's reactions without a title card, so feeling is shown not said; the camera watching a watcher recurs (Pleasure Garden binoculars)
- **extended** (ch-007 long take and sound): Spoto: Murder! (1930) first long unbroken take (three minutes, two women moving room to room); to give an interior monologue before dubbing existed Hitchcock played a pre-recorded wire monologue off camera and a 30-piece orchestra live while the actor shaved. Rich and Strange opens on a long crane shot over an office. Theatre used as a frame for playing versus being
- **extended** (ch-010 point of view and motif): Spoto on Sabotage: a subjective dissolve (fish tank to imagined explosion and back) shows a character's thought in the frame; one image family (birds, meals with carving knives, the cinema) is planted early and recurs so a late moment pays off; ambiguous action (Verloc seems to walk into the knife) is staged to show dual intention; the audience is made partly accomplice
- **extended** (ch-023 casting and coverage): Spoto on The Paradine Case: five cameras were positioned for the courtroom scenes so tension could be recorded without constantly resetting (multi-camera coverage); a high-key light makes the leading woman's face masklike; alternating sequences between two women reveal the man's character; a subjective-objective shot places the wife behind wooden bars to show imprisonment; casting an appealing actor makes the audience share his illusion
- **extended** (ch-028 subjective flashback): Spoto on I Confess: a woman's account of her past is shown from her own viewpoint with slow motion, soft focus and unbalanced angles plus the romantic theme song, so the look shows the fantasy rather than endorsing it; a priest's silence is a scene of pure restraint; the first confession in a dark booth is mirrored by a public one on a stage. The look of a flashback can say whose memory it is and how reliable
- **extended** (ch-029 filmed play and film time): Spoto on Dial M for Murder: a one-set play adapted by tightening and focusing the text and adding close-ups, silences, colour and props; the murder attempt crosscuts the killer's wait, the watch, and the phone's inner mechanism to stretch a few seconds of real time and make the audience impatient on the killer's side; colour of costume changes with the heroine's fortunes. Compare lesson 4 on adapting a play for the screen
- **extended** (ch-033 sequence design): Spoto on the Albert Hall sequence of The Man Who Knew Too Much (1956): wordless, about twelve minutes and 124 shots; suspense built from the decision in one character's will (scream and save the target, or stay silent and save her son), not from external action; crosscutting balanced in three sets of three (orchestra, killer group, targets), shots arranged in an ordered survey of the hall, repeated red and black-and-white colour links; the mother's tear-stained face is cut to about twelve times. Strong model for the case study lesson on rhythm and the cut
- **extended** (ch-035 trick shots and in-camera effects): Spoto (Hitchcock's own account): the ghostly green emergence of Judy was made with a wide sliding glass in front of the camera, blurred at the top and raised as she approached, plus a green hotel sign; the room-to-stable dissolve used a circular set, a 360-degree camera pass projected on a screen with the actors on a turntable; the falls used double printing/travelling matte. Practical, low-tech effects planned with the lens and set
- **extended** (ch-038 planning rhythm on paper): Spoto on The Birds: Hitchcock attached wide sheets of paper to his office walls graphing the rise and fall of each sequence and the alternation of dialogue with action, and tied each attack to the exact emotional line that precedes it; over fourteen hundred shots (more than twice the usual) and a three-year preparation with effects, trained birds and composite work. Plan the rhythm of a whole film as a chart; couple each big moment to a human cause
- **note** (ch-031 visual jokes): Spoto on To Catch a Thief: a cliche image (fireworks during a love scene) is used as an open visual joke; a mirrored action (lights switched off one by one against lights switched on in Rear Window) links scenes. Colour location photography won an Oscar. No course change
- **note** (ch-046 filmography): Spoto: credits and bibliography only; confirms the long working partnership with the same cinematographers, designers and writers across films. No course change

### directing-3

- **extended** (ch-006 Blackmail sound): Spoto: Hitchcock 'designed the sound' of Blackmail, distorting a neighbour's chatter so only 'knife' stabs through, to render Alice's subjective state; birds as motif for disorder; early sound forced an actress's lines to be spoken off camera by another actress. A director shapes what the audience hears as well as sees
- **extended** (ch-008 through-line): Spoto on The 39 Steps: one theme (trust and betrayal, appearance against reality) governs every sequence; three pairs of couples illuminate it (Hannay and Pamela, crofter and wife, innkeeper and wife) and a repeated gesture (the supper offered three times) ties scenes together; the film begins and ends in a theatre. A clear through-line and balanced parallels make a comic thriller feel unified
- **extended** (ch-019 doubling and through-line): Spoto on Shadow of a Doubt: the opening is a paired double sequence (two cities, two houses, two bedrooms, two characters lying on beds) that states the theme before any dialogue; a long list of doubles and echoes ties the two Charlies; the central dark-night scene is lit so faces are indistinct. A director can build a through-line from deliberate pairs and repeats. Also: a performance built out of listening (Teresa Wright is an acute listener) and filming out of sequence demands an actor who holds the arc
- **extended** (ch-043 directing on set): Spoto's interviews with Family Plot's cast and crew: the director explained what each shot was meant to say and what the actor had to do, left room only for the actor's freshness, calmly prepared everything before the set day, and held an audience in mind for each detail; an actor was given an image to keep a light tone and 'played the clothes'; the cinematographer says he asked the lens, knew what would appear on screen, and never moved the camera without a reason; the costume designer was told the answer was in the script. A concrete model of clear direction plus calm preparation, for lesson 4 on the film set
- **note** (ch-032 tone and understatement): Spoto on The Trouble with Harry: understatement is the method (characters treat a corpse matter-of-factly, set in bright autumn rather than night); the film is deliberately ambiguous between two readings, and the book warns critics against over-reading symbols into a work. A director fixes a tone and keeps characters playing it straight

### directing-1

- **extended** (ch-007 structure and MacGuffin): Spoto: Man Who Knew Too Much (1934) is built on planted setups paid off at the end (skeet match returns as the rooftop shot; ski slope to sloping roof); set up a detail early so the ending feels inevitable. The MacGuffin is only the pretext, the story is about personal feeling; terror placed in glamorous or respectable settings
- **extended** (ch-011 bookend and motif): Spoto on Young and Innocent: opening and closing images are exact reversals (shouting brunette to smiling blonde; argument to reconciliation); a visual motif (eyes, glasses, blindfold) carries the ethic; 'content determines technique': the 200-foot crane from ballroom to the murderer's twitching eyes works because it ties us to a clue. Supports finding the theme and turning it into a look
- **extended** (ch-022 structure and subtext): Spoto on Notorious: the first five scene elements are mirrored in reverse in the last five (a planned 'table of contents'), so the ending answers the opening; a drink motif runs through the film; gestures carry two meanings (an embrace used as a ruse), which gives playable subtext; a crane from a grand foyer to a key in a hand puts two levels of reality in one image; final love scene uses no music. Design the bookends and the motif before shooting
- **extended** (ch-033 remake and opening image): Spoto: the remake deepens characters and makes the marriage the real subject (the MacGuffin is the plot pretext); the first image (the boy between his parents) is reversed in the last; a song is planted early and reused to rescue the child. Planting a payoff early; reworking a text to put the relationship at its centre
- **extended** (ch-035 theme into look): Spoto on Vertigo: the spiral is the one image from which the whole look derives (title design, stair, hair, car routes, camera circles); the camera pans right-to-left in the first half and left-to-right in the second; recurring red and green; every sound cue was marked in the script; the screenwriter says the story was worked out and the screenwriter's job was to personalise characters and dialogue (he invented Midge). Strong model for turning a theme into a look and for collaboration with a writer
- **extended** (ch-035 audience choice: suspense over surprise): Spoto on Vertigo: Hitchcock reveals Judy's secret mid-film (a letter read in voice-over while the camera half-circles her) and sacrifices surprise for suspense so the audience watches Scottie rather than with him and must judge its own responses; colour pairs (red and green) were planned in the shooting script and notes, and the cemetery scene was diffused deliberately to 'put a feeling onto it'. A director decides what the audience knows and when; knowledge in the audience is a design choice
- **extended** (ch-042 one governing metaphor): Spoto on Frenzy: a single metaphor (food and appetite) governs props, settings, dialogue and an early line of speech that later pays off (a spoken promise of clean water, followed at once by a floating body); lines added late to the screenplay deepen it. A controlling image gives the whole film a theme the designer, writer and actors can all serve
- **note** (ch-012 coming in late): Spoto: Hitchcock took over The Lady Vanishes after script and cast were set and still added 'grace notes and one major motif'; every minor character's quirk carries the theme of appearance against reality. Casting and small characterful details each serve the theme
- **note** (ch-026 theatre as subject): Spoto on Stage Fright: an actress-heroine succeeds by playing roles for real, so a rehearsal-room skill (playing a part with conviction) becomes the plot; the opening safety curtain rises on real London; an opening lying flashback is a risky choice that annoyed viewers. Useful illustration of acting as the story's engine; no change planned
- **note** (ch-040 look without feeling): Spoto on Torn Curtain: controlled colour (red in every frame, a gray gauze over the lens) and a strong fire motif could not rescue a film judged short of emotional power, with characters as ciphers; a technical concept needs an emotional spine. Hitchcock sketched the frame in the air to show actors what fills the screen

### directing-2

- **extended** (ch-009 objectives reverse): Spoto on Secret Agent: two characters swap moral positions halfway (Elsa begins eager, Ashenden reluctant; then she objects and he acts), so each character's want changes under pressure; sound motifs (bells, sirens, whirring belts) escalate toward the climax. Shows a change in objective across a play, relevant to units and super-objective
- **extended** (ch-015 working with actors): Spoto: Hitchcock gave Albert Bassermann, who learned his lines phonetically without English, a quick summary of each scene just before he went on camera, and the performance was acute; Benchley wrote his own dialogue and was welcomed. A director feeds each actor only the context needed for the moment. Also a recurring prop (the bowler hat) as punctuation: a repeated object carries a theme
- **extended** (ch-021 actor's director): Spoto on Spellbound: despite the 'actors are cattle' joke, Hitchcock made an atmosphere in which restrained, natural performances could emerge, 'never overdirecting' and not intruding on the actor's understanding of a moment; he varied image size, placement against background and lighting to suit the emotional need of the shot, and faced both actors toward camera so the audience feels both reactions. A director's visual choices serve the actor. Contrast the Stanislavski lessons
- **extended** (ch-036 role-playing as subject): Spoto on North by Northwest: the script is full of performance language (an actor-style critique: 'a little less training from the FBI and a little more from the Actors Studio'), so playing a role is the story; numbers and small props (a hidden 13, the bourbon/gin joke) are late grace notes added to the script; the opening scene sketches character in dictation, bribes and a stolen taxi. Character shown through action in the first minutes
- **extended** (ch-039 actor and trauma): Spoto on Marnie: a leading performance built on understatement and calm against hysterical material (Tippi Hedren in only her second film), with a childlike falsetto for the remembered trauma; the film works through repeated gestures ('There, there now' at the horse and at the memory) and red colour flashes that mean the repressed memory. A reminder that the actor's inner objective can be given a physical, repeated action that triggers the past (compare emotion memory)

### directing-4

- **extended** (ch-014 placement in frame): Spoto on Rebecca: the heroine is held to the extreme right of the frame, nearly pushed out by the overbearing woman and the glamorous man, to show her lack of power; repeated identical glance by two dominating women links them. Staging and frame position carry status. Also 'cutting in the camera' (shooting lean) so a producer and editor are left only the wanted material
- **extended** (ch-017 character through staging): Spoto on Suspicion: Lina's whole character is sketched in three shots (tiny figure before a window in a formal room, medium close-up turning magazine pages, close-up of delicate face); small business (removing her glasses, snapping her handbag shut) shows feeling without words; a scene is repeated exactly at the end with new meaning; the camera shows the story from one neurotic viewpoint. Shot size and business reveal inner life
- **extended** (ch-020 confined space): Spoto on Lifeboat: the whole film is limited to the narrowest acting space (a lifeboat) as a deliberate technical challenge, with no music except under the titles and only wind and waves; a character's arc is shown by what she loses object by object (camera, coat, typewriter, bracelet). Limits can drive invention; progressive stripping of props shows change
- **extended** (ch-034 camera height as pressure): Spoto on The Wrong Man: shot on real locations in black-and-white, with high and low angles instead of eye level so the world feels off-centre as Manny's trouble grows; a broken-mirror shot splits an image to show a broken mind; flat, banal dialogue makes tragedy more painful; the studio added a happy ending over the director's objection. Use of angle and setting to show a character's state

### directing-6

- **extended** (ch-041 preparation and colour design): Spoto on Topaz: shot while the script was being written a few days ahead of each scene, and a film that normally had every element planned in advance (writer secluded until the script was perfected, then designers, wardrobe, crew) suffered; the screenwriter said more time would have made it better. Colour was assigned by character and nation (yellow for French, red for Communist, lavender for tenderness and death) in production files with the designer; a staircase murder was staged with a circling then overhead camera and wire spokes in the gown
- **note** (ch-018 budget limits): Spoto on Saboteur: money spent on script revisions and expensive setups left cheap backdrops, miniatures and rear projection; the director also had to settle for cheaper leads. Shows the budget trade-off between preparation and the shoot; a single motif (fire against water) was chosen at the start to unify
